items.prompt: What is a "query plan"?
choices: The specific sequence of steps a database follows to execute a given query
The schema diagram showing every table in a database
A written document describing future database migrations
The list of users who have permission to query a table
items.explanation: A query plan is the concrete execution strategy a database chooses for a specific query — not a schema diagram, migration doc, or permissions list.

items.prompt: Can two queries that look similar have very different performance as data grows?
choices: Yes — different query plans can scale very differently even for superficially similar queries
No — if two queries return similar-looking results, their performance is always identical
No — query performance depends only on the total size of the database, never on the specific query
Yes, but only if the queries are written in different programming languages
items.explanation: The underlying plan, not just the surface shape of the query, is what determines how performance scales — two similar-looking queries can have very different plans.

items.prompt: What is the "N+1 query problem"?
choices: Fetching a list with one query, then issuing one additional query per item in that list to fetch related data
A database that requires exactly N+1 tables to store all its data
A query that returns N+1 rows instead of the expected N rows
A bug where a query runs exactly once too many times due to a retry
items.explanation: N+1 specifically describes 1 query for a list plus N follow-up queries (one per item) — not a row-count mismatch, a retry bug, or a table-count requirement.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, why does query count scale with the number of orders specifically?
choices: The code issues one additional customer lookup for every order in the list, on top of the one query that fetches the order list itself
Each order requires exactly two queries regardless of how the code is written
The database re-runs the entire query plan from scratch for every order
Query count doesn't actually scale with order count — the slowdown is caused by something else entirely
items.explanation: Each order in the list triggers its own separate customer lookup — that per-order cost is exactly what makes total query count grow with the number of orders.

items.prompt: What does "normalization" mean in this unit's context?
choices: Structuring data so each fact is stored in exactly one place, avoiding duplication at the cost of needing joins or extra lookups
Converting all text fields in a database to lowercase
Compressing a database file to save disk space
Removing all indexes from a table to simplify its structure
items.explanation: Normalization is about eliminating duplicated facts by storing each one in a single place — not about text formatting, compression, or removing indexes.

items.prompt: In a normalized schema, where does a customer's name live?
choices: Only in the customers table — orders reference the customer by id and look up the name when needed
Duplicated on every order that customer has ever placed
In a separate file outside the database entirely
Nowhere — normalized schemas don't store customer names at all
items.explanation: Normalization keeps a fact like a customer's name in exactly one place (the customers table), with other tables referencing it by id rather than duplicating it.

items.prompt: What does "denormalization" mean?
choices: Deliberately duplicating some data to avoid needing a join or extra lookup, at the cost of keeping the duplicates in sync
Removing all foreign key constraints from a database
Splitting a single table into many smaller normalized tables
Storing data in a format that can't be queried directly
items.explanation: Denormalization is specifically about trading duplication (and the sync burden that comes with it) for faster reads — not about constraints, table-splitting, or unqueryable formats.

items.prompt: If a system denormalizes a customer's name onto every order, what new responsibility does that create?
choices: Every place that could rename a customer now has to also update every order that duplicated the old name
The system no longer needs a customers table at all
Orders can no longer be queried by customer id
The database automatically keeps the duplicated names in sync with no extra code needed
items.explanation: Duplicated data doesn't stay in sync automatically — any code path that changes the original has to be updated to also change every duplicate, or the copies drift.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, did the code or the database schema change between the fast dev result and the slow production result?
choices: No — neither changed; only the amount of data (number of orders) changed
Yes — the production database used a completely different schema than dev
Yes — the code was rewritten before deploying to production
It's impossible to tell from the Scenario's facts
items.explanation: The Scenario explicitly states the code and schema were unchanged — the only thing that changed was the volume of data, which is what exposed the N+1 pattern's cost.

items.prompt: Why did the Scenario's slowdown stay invisible during development with only 20 orders?
choices: 21 total queries (1 + 20) is fast enough in absolute terms that the per-order cost pattern wasn't noticeable at that scale
The N+1 pattern only exists in production environments, never in development
Development databases automatically batch queries that production databases don't
The bug didn't actually exist in the dev version of the code
items.explanation: At small scale, even an inefficient pattern can be fast enough in absolute terms to go unnoticed — the same pattern's cost becomes visible once the list size (and thus the query count) grows large.

items.prompt: Per L2, what actually scales with the number of orders in the Scenario's endpoint?
choices: The number of queries issued per request
The raw processing speed of the database server
The size of the database's disk storage
The number of indexes defined on the orders table
items.explanation: L2 identifies query count — not database speed, storage size, or index count — as the thing that grows in direct proportion to the number of orders.

items.prompt: Per L2's diagram, how many total queries does listing 50,000 orders with an N+1 pattern require?
choices: 50,001 — one query for the order list plus one per-order customer lookup
Exactly 2, regardless of how many orders there are
50,000, since the initial order-list query doesn't count separately
1, since all the lookups happen within a single database connection
items.explanation: The pattern is 1 query for the list plus N queries (one per item) — for 50,000 orders, that's 50,001 total queries, matching L2's diagram exactly.

items.prompt: Per L2, would upgrading to a faster database server fully fix the Scenario's N+1 slowdown?
choices: Only partially — it reduces the cost per query, but the total delay still scales linearly with the number of orders either way
Yes — a fast enough server eliminates any performance difference caused by query count
No — a faster server would have no effect on this problem at all
Yes, but only if the server is upgraded at the same time the schema is redesigned
items.explanation: A faster server helps each individual query, but doesn't change the structural fact that total query count scales with list size — the underlying pattern still needs fixing.

items.prompt: Why does L2 say the database was never "slow" in isolation in the Scenario?
choices: Because each individual query could still be fast — the actual problem was the code asking for 50,001 separate small things instead of one larger one
Because the database in the Scenario had no performance issues whatsoever, even before any fix
Because "slow" is not a meaningful term to apply to any database under any circumstances
Because the slowdown was actually caused by network issues unrelated to querying
items.explanation: L2 frames the issue as a query-count problem, not a raw-speed problem — each query could be individually fast while the total pattern still produces a severe delay.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, what does a normalized schema optimize for, and what does it cost?
choices: It optimizes for simple writes (updating a fact in one place); it costs reads needing a join or extra lookup for related data
It optimizes for fast reads; it costs extra disk space
It optimizes for fast writes and fast reads simultaneously, with no real cost
It optimizes for security; it costs query flexibility
items.explanation: L2's table specifically pairs normalization with simple, single-location writes and a read-side cost (joins/lookups) — not security or a free lunch on both reads and writes.

items.prompt: Per L2, is denormalization simply the better approach whenever it's an option?
choices: No — each approach is the right answer for a different access pattern; the choice depends on how often reads vs. writes to that data actually happen
Yes — denormalization is always strictly better than normalization for any system
No — denormalization should never be used under any circumstances
Yes, but only for databases with fewer than 1,000 rows
items.explanation: L2 explicitly frames this as a trade-off dependent on the actual access pattern (read frequency vs. write/rename frequency), not a universal preference for either approach.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, does adding an index fix an N+1 query pattern?
choices: No — an index helps a single query find data faster, but does nothing about a query pattern that issues N+1 separate queries in the first place
Yes — adding an index always eliminates N+1 query patterns entirely
Yes, but only if the index is added to every table in the database
No, because indexes only apply to write operations, never to reads
items.explanation: L2 explicitly separates the concerns: an index speeds up finding data within one query, while N+1 is a problem with how many separate queries get issued in the first place.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's risky about denormalizing data without a plan for keeping duplicates in sync?
choices: The duplicated copies can quietly drift out of sync with the original if not every write path is updated to keep them consistent
There's no real risk — duplicated data is always automatically kept in sync by the database
It's risky only because it uses more disk space, not because of any correctness issue
It's risky only in databases that don't support foreign keys
items.explanation: L2 warns specifically about sync drift — duplicated data needs every relevant write path updated, or the copies silently become inconsistent with the source of truth.

items.prompt: Fix listOrdersWithCustomerJoined so it looks up all customers in a single pass (building a Map) instead of querying per order, keeping the total query count at 1 regardless of order count.

tests.description: query count stays at 1 regardless of order count
tests.expr: expect((() => { queryCount = 0; const db = { customers: [{ id: 1, name: "Alice" }, { id: 2, name: "Bob" }], orders: [{ id: 1, customerId: 1 }, { id: 2, customerId: 1 }, { id: 3, customerId: 2 }] }; listOrdersWithCustomerJoined(db); return queryCount; })()).toBe(1)

tests.description: each order gets the correct customer name attached
tests.expr: expect((() => { queryCount = 0; const db = { customers: [{ id: 1, name: "Alice" }, { id: 2, name: "Bob" }], orders: [{ id: 1, customerId: 2 }] }; return listOrdersWithCustomerJoined(db)[0].customerName; })()).toBe("Bob")

items.explanation: Building one Map from every customer's id to their record costs a single query, and looking up each order's customer from that in-memory Map costs nothing extra in query count — no matter how many orders there are, the total stays at 1.
items.reference:
❌ N+1 — one related-record lookup per item, scales with list size
✅ Joined — one lookup for all related records, constant regardless of list size

Why: fetching related data together, not one row at a time, is what breaks the linear scaling.

items.prompt: Fix listProductsWithCategoryJoined so it looks up all categories in a single pass (building a Map) instead of querying per product, keeping the total query count at 1 regardless of product count.

tests.description: query count stays at 1 regardless of product count
tests.expr: expect((() => { queryCount = 0; const db = { categories: [{ id: 1, name: "Tools" }], products: [{ id: 1, categoryId: 1 }, { id: 2, categoryId: 1 }] }; listProductsWithCategoryJoined(db); return queryCount; })()).toBe(1)

tests.description: each product gets the correct category name attached
tests.expr: expect((() => { queryCount = 0; const db = { categories: [{ id: 1, name: "Tools" }, { id: 2, name: "Hardware" }], products: [{ id: 1, categoryId: 2 }] }; return listProductsWithCategoryJoined(db)[0].categoryName; })()).toBe("Hardware")

items.explanation: Same fix regardless of the domain: build one lookup Map for all related records in a single query, and resolve each item's related data from that in-memory Map instead of issuing a separate query per item.
items.reference:
❌ N+1 — one related-record lookup per item, scales with list size
✅ Joined — one lookup for all related records, constant regardless of list size

Why: fetching related data together, not one row at a time, is what breaks the linear scaling.

items.prompt: Fix renameCustomer so that renaming a customer also updates the duplicated customerName on every one of their orders, keeping the denormalized copies in sync.

tests.description: the customer record itself is renamed
tests.expr: expect((() => { const db = { customers: [{ id: 1, name: "Alice" }], orders: [{ id: 1, customerId: 1, customerName: "Alice" }] }; renameCustomer(db, 1, "Alicia"); return db.customers[0].name; })()).toBe("Alicia")

tests.description: every order belonging to that customer has its duplicated name updated too
tests.expr: expect((() => { const db = { customers: [{ id: 1, name: "Alice" }], orders: [{ id: 1, customerId: 1, customerName: "Alice" }, { id: 2, customerId: 1, customerName: "Alice" }] }; renameCustomer(db, 1, "Alicia"); return db.orders.every((o) => o.customerName === "Alicia"); })()).toBe(true)

tests.description: orders belonging to a different customer are untouched
tests.expr: expect((() => { const db = { customers: [{ id: 1, name: "Alice" }, { id: 2, name: "Bob" }], orders: [{ id: 1, customerId: 1, customerName: "Alice" }, { id: 2, customerId: 2, customerName: "Bob" }] }; renameCustomer(db, 1, "Alicia"); return db.orders[1].customerName; })()).toBe("Bob")

items.explanation: Because the customer's name was deliberately duplicated onto every order for fast reads, the write path that changes the original now has to walk every order belonging to that customer and update the duplicate too — that's the ongoing cost denormalization trades for faster reads.
items.reference:
📖 Fast read — the duplicated field is already on the related record, no lookup needed
✏️ Slower write — a rename now has to update every duplicated copy

Why: denormalized data only stays correct if every write path that changes the source also updates the copies.

items.prompt: Fix renameCategory so that renaming a category also updates the duplicated categoryName on every product in that category, keeping the denormalized copies in sync.

tests.description: the category record itself is renamed
tests.expr: expect((() => { const db = { categories: [{ id: 1, name: "Tools" }], products: [{ id: 1, categoryId: 1, categoryName: "Tools" }] }; renameCategory(db, 1, "Hardware"); return db.categories[0].name; })()).toBe("Hardware")

tests.description: every product in that category has its duplicated name updated too
tests.expr: expect((() => { const db = { categories: [{ id: 1, name: "Tools" }], products: [{ id: 1, categoryId: 1, categoryName: "Tools" }, { id: 2, categoryId: 1, categoryName: "Tools" }] }; renameCategory(db, 1, "Hardware"); return db.products.every((p) => p.categoryName === "Hardware"); })()).toBe(true)

tests.description: products in a different category are untouched
tests.expr: expect((() => { const db = { categories: [{ id: 1, name: "Tools" }, { id: 2, name: "Books" }], products: [{ id: 1, categoryId: 1, categoryName: "Tools" }, { id: 2, categoryId: 2, categoryName: "Books" }] }; renameCategory(db, 1, "Hardware"); return db.products[1].categoryName; })()).toBe("Books")

items.explanation: Same fix as any denormalized-field rename: walk every record that duplicated the old value and update it alongside the source, or the copies silently drift out of sync.
items.reference:
📖 Fast read — the duplicated field is already on the related record, no lookup needed
✏️ Slower write — a rename now has to update every duplicated copy

Why: denormalized data only stays correct if every write path that changes the source also updates the copies.
